stem: Which of the following is a typical objective of testing as defined in the CTFL syllabus?
options: To prove the absence of all defects.
To provide information to stakeholders about the quality of the test object.
To debug the code so it compiles successfully.
To produce a faster build pipeline.
explanation: Providing information about quality so stakeholders can make informed decisions is one of the canonical objectives. Testing cannot prove absence of defects; debugging is a developer activity; build performance is unrelated.

stem: After a developer fixes a defect, who typically performs the confirmation test and what does it verify?
options: The developer; it verifies the fix compiles.
The tester; it verifies the originally-failing test now passes with the same inputs.
The product owner; it verifies the user accepts the fix.
explanation: Confirmation testing is a tester activity that re-runs the original failing test to verify the defect has been fixed. The developer debugs; confirmation testing is part of testing, not debugging.

stem: Which sequence correctly describes the cause-and-effect chain in the testing terminology of mistake, defect, and failure?
options: Failure -> Defect -> Mistake (a failure causes a defect which causes a mistake).
Mistake -> Defect -> Failure (a person's mistake creates a defect that, when executed, may produce a failure).
explanation: A human mistake (error) introduces a defect (fault, bug) in a work product; executing the defective code may produce a failure (observable wrong behaviour). The chain runs in that order; the three terms are distinct.

stem: Which statement correctly relates Quality Assurance (QA), Quality Control (QC), and testing?
options: QA, QC, and testing are synonyms.
Testing is a form of QC, which is product-focused; QA is process-focused.
QA is performed only by managers; QC only by developers.
QC replaces the need for QA in modern teams.
explanation: QA is about the process producing quality; QC is about checking the product; testing is a specific QC activity. Mature organisations use both.

stem: A test team has run the same regression suite weekly for a year and finds almost no new defects. Which testing principle does this illustrate?
options: Pesticide paradox - tests wear out and need to be revised.
explanation: The pesticide paradox states that running the same tests repeatedly stops finding new defects. The team must review and add new tests.

stem: During which test activity is each abstract test condition elaborated into a concrete test case with specific inputs, expected results, and preconditions?
explanation: Test design turns abstract test conditions (identified during analysis) into concrete test cases. Implementation prepares the data/environment; execution runs the tests.

stem: A regulator asks the team to prove that every requirement in v3.0 has been tested. Which testware property is MOST critical?
options: Traceability between requirements and test cases.
explanation: Requirement-to-test traceability is the property that lets you demonstrate, requirement-by-requirement, what was tested and with what result.

stem: In the V-model, which test level is paired with the system requirements specification?
explanation: The V-model pairs acceptance testing with the original business/system requirements. System testing is paired with system design; integration with architecture; component with detailed design.

stem: Which approach describes BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development)?
options: Developers write failing unit tests before any production code.
Business, dev, and tester agree on Given/When/Then behaviour scenarios that double as executable tests and documentation.
Static code analysis on every commit.
explanation: BDD uses Given/When/Then Gherkin scenarios, typically co-authored by business + dev + tester, executed via tools like Cucumber. They serve as both tests and living documentation.

stem: A defect is found where two microservices fail to communicate because one sends XML while the other expects JSON. Which test level is MOST appropriate for finding this?
explanation: Interface-format mismatches between two services is the canonical target of integration testing. Component testing isolates units; system and acceptance testing might catch downstream symptoms but are not the right level.

stem: After a developer fixes defect #500, what should the tester do before the defect can be closed?
options: Confirmation testing to verify the fix, then regression testing to verify nothing else broke.
No additional testing - closing the defect is enough.
explanation: Confirmation testing re-runs the originally failing test. Regression testing verifies that the fix did not break other parts of the system. Both are necessary before closure.

stem: An organisation patches a security vulnerability in its production system without otherwise changing functionality. Which type of maintenance testing is MOST relevant?
explanation: Patching a security vulnerability is corrective maintenance (fixing a defect - the security weakness). Adaptive responds to environment changes; perfective adds new features; preventive refactors for future cost reduction.

stem: Which ISO 25010 quality characteristic is BEST associated with a test that measures system availability over a 30-day continuous run?
explanation: Availability is a sub-characteristic of reliability in ISO/IEC 25010. Functional suitability is about correctness; portability is about installability/adaptability; maintainability is about modifiability.

stem: Which of the following is a static testing activity?
options: Running unit tests against a freshly built binary.
Reviewing a requirements document for ambiguity.
Acceptance testing by an end user.
explanation: Static testing examines work products without execution. Reviewing a requirements document is static. Running unit tests, performance testing, and acceptance testing all execute the software (dynamic).

stem: Which review type is the MOST formal, with defined entry/exit criteria, pre-assigned roles (moderator, author, reader, scribe, reviewer), and metric collection?
explanation: Inspection is the most formal review type, used where high rigor is needed (safety-critical, contractual). The other types are progressively less formal.

stem: A team holds a 3-hour review meeting of a large design document and is dissatisfied with the few defects found. Which improvement is MOST likely to help?
options: Skip the review and rely on dynamic testing.
Split the document into smaller chunks and have reviewers prepare beforehand.
Replace the moderator with the document's author.
explanation: Manageable scope and individual preparation are key success factors. Long meetings without preparation lead to fatigue and missed defects. The author leading the meeting would reduce independence.

stem: A team wants reviewers to find a balanced mix of security, usability, and testability defects in a requirements document. Which review technique BEST suits this?
explanation: Perspective-based review assigns each reviewer a distinct lens (security, usability, testability), diversifying findings. Ad-hoc relies on luck; inspection is a review type, not a technique to diversify perspectives; static analysis is a tool-based approach.

stem: A tester designs test cases by partitioning the input domain into valid and invalid partitions, without reference to the internal source code. Which category of technique is this?
explanation: Equivalence partitioning of the input domain from the specification, without code access, is black-box. White-box uses code structure; experience-based uses tester intuition; risk-based is a prioritisation approach.

stem: A form accepts integers 1-100. Using equivalence partitioning, what is the MINIMUM number of partitions to test for full partition coverage?
options: 3 - the valid range plus invalid-low and invalid-high.
explanation: EP for a numeric range gives three partitions: valid [1..100], invalid below (< 1), invalid above (> 100). Each needs at least one representative test.

stem: A field accepts integers 10 to 50. Using two-value BVA, which set of values should be tested?
explanation: Two-value BVA tests the boundary and the value just outside the partition at each end: 9 (just-outside-low), 10 (boundary-low), 50 (boundary-high), 51 (just-outside-high). Three-value would include 11 and 49 as well.

stem: A system's behaviour is driven by 4 boolean conditions. How many rules does the FULL (uncollapsed) decision table have?
explanation: With n boolean conditions, the full decision table has 2^n rules. 2^4 = 16. Full coverage requires one test per rule.

stem: A state transition diagram has 5 states and 12 transitions. What is the minimum number of transitions exercised for all-transitions (0-switch) coverage?
explanation: All-transitions (0-switch) coverage exercises every transition at least once: 12 transitions -> minimum 12. Multiple transitions may be covered by a single test that walks several states, but the transition count itself is 12.

stem: Given `if (x > 0) print('a'); print('b');` and a test with x = 5, the print('b') always runs. Which statement is true?
explanation: x=5 makes the if-condition true, so both prints execute (100% statement coverage). Only one of two branches (the true branch) was taken (50% branch coverage). This illustrates that statement coverage is strictly weaker than branch coverage.

stem: Which scenario is MOST suitable for exploratory testing?
options: Running stable nightly regression on a 5-year-old product.
Investigating a newly-built feature whose acceptance criteria are still evolving.
Audit-quality testing of a regulated medical device.
explanation: Exploratory testing shines when the system is new and specs are evolving - the tester uses curiosity and emerging understanding to find defects. Stable regression suits scripted automation; regulated audit testing prefers documented scripted tests.

stem: BA, developer, and tester meet before a story enters development to agree on concrete acceptance examples. What is this practice called?
explanation: The three amigos practice has business, development, and testing perspectives collaboratively define acceptance examples for each story before implementation.

stem: Why is Modified Condition / Decision Coverage (MC/DC) chosen in safety-critical avionics software?
options: It is mandated by regulatory standards (e.g., DO-178C Level A).
It replaces all other testing techniques.
explanation: MC/DC is mandated by safety-critical standards like DO-178C Level A. It is rigorous and expensive; it does not replace other techniques and does not guarantee zero defects.

stem: Which is the BEST example of an EXIT criterion for system testing?
options: All severity-1 defects resolved; required coverage achieved; open defects accepted by stakeholders.
explanation: Exit criteria gate the *end* of testing - resolution of high-severity defects, coverage achievement, and stakeholder acceptance of open defects are typical exit criteria. The other items are entry criteria.

stem: Using PERT (three-point) estimation with optimistic 3 days, most likely 5 days, pessimistic 13 days, what is the expected effort?
Which of the following is BEST classified as a project risk (not a product risk)?
options: A defect in the payment module could lose customer money.
The test environment may be unavailable for the integration test window.
The login screen may have a SQL injection vulnerability.
The checkout page may fail to meet the 2-second SLA.
explanation: Test environment availability is a *project* risk - it threatens the team's ability to deliver testing. The other items are potential product defects (product risks) addressed by testing.

stem: Which area MOST deserves additional testing effort under risk-based testing?
options: The credit card payment processing module.
An internal admin tool with two users.
explanation: Payment processing has high impact (financial, regulatory, reputational) and non-trivial likelihood of defects. The other items have far lower impact and warrant lighter testing.

stem: Which risk assessment technique uses a Risk Priority Number = Severity x Occurrence x Detection?
explanation: FMEA (Failure Modes and Effects Analysis) uses the RPN = Severity x Occurrence x Detection formula.

stem: Which metric BEST measures how effective a test level is at catching defects before later levels?
explanation: DDP = (defects found at this level) / (defects found at this level + later levels). High DDP means the level catches most defects before they escape downstream.

stem: Severity and priority of a defect are:
options: Two names for the same property.
Severity is impact; priority is urgency - independent properties.
explanation: Severity is about impact (how badly the defect affects the system/users); priority is about urgency (how quickly it must be fixed). They are independent - a severe defect in an unused feature may have low priority.

stem: A defect found on Monday cannot be reproduced on Tuesday after 12 commits and an environment rebuild. Which configuration management practice would BEST help?
options: Tagging the build, testware, and environment configuration at the time of the defect.
Reducing the number of automated tests.
explanation: Tagging the exact combination lets the team return to that baseline to reproduce and diagnose the defect.

stem: A team picks the 30 regression tests that cover recently-changed modules to run on tonight's release. Which prioritisation strategy is this?
explanation: Selecting tests covering recently-changed code is recency-based prioritisation - based on where regression is most likely.

stem: Which tool category is BEST suited to issuing HTTP requests to an API and asserting on the JSON response?
options: API testing tool (e.g., Postman, REST Assured).
explanation: API testing tools issue requests and assert responses. Test management tools track work; static analysers examine source; performance tools measure load characteristics.

stem: Which is generally the BEST candidate for test automation?
options: Exploratory testing of a new feature with unstable acceptance criteria.
A stable, frequently-run regression check for a critical workflow.
Subjective usability evaluation by an expert.
explanation: Frequent, stable regression pays back automation investment quickly. Exploratory and subjective tasks need humans; one-time work does not pay back the cost.

stem: A team has many flaky automated tests. What is the MOST important action?
options: Diagnose and fix or delete each flaky test; flakiness destroys trust in the whole suite.
Add more tests to dilute the impact.
Abandon automation and revert to manual.
explanation: Flaky tests train teams to ignore failures. Each flaky test must be investigated and fixed (e.g., proper waits, deterministic data) or deleted. Diluting and abandoning are anti-patterns.

stem: A team wants non-programmer testers to author automated tests while a developer maintains the underlying code. Which approach BEST fits?
explanation: Keyword-driven testing lets non-programmers compose tests from high-level keywords; programmers maintain the underlying keyword implementations.

stem: An organisation selected a new test automation tool. What is the MOST important activity before rolling it out to all teams?
options: Bulk-buy licences to lock in pricing.
Pilot the tool on a small, representative real project; capture lessons.
Re-brand the tool with the company logo.
Disable existing test frameworks to force adoption.
explanation: A pilot on a real but small project reveals fit, gaps, and effort before company-wide commitment. Bulk-buying before piloting risks shelf-ware; cosmetics and forced adoption don't address fit or skill gaps.
